name: com.cuvara.netcode
description: Client wire transport, codec, two-hop handshake (gateway → game server), snapshot resolution and world state management for the RPG MMO.

x-optionalDependencies.jp.hadashikick.vcontainer: 1.16.8 — enables Cuvara.Netcode.DI and Cuvara.Netcode.Bootstrap; absent, those assemblies are excluded and the rest of the package is unaffected

samples.description: Dev harness scene that runs the full gateway → game server → enter world → input/snapshot loop against a local backend.

Renders replicated entities as primitive GameObjects so the world can be looked at rather than read from logs. Run one in a player build and one in the Editor to see two clients move around each other. No interpolation and no prediction, on purpose.

Client-driven certification rig: Nakama device auth and the gateway_token RPC, both handshake hops, the input/snapshot loop, resync, and a reconnect inside the server's 30 s entity hold. Needs a running backend and no signing secret.

Full client against a live backend, presented with DOTS/ECS: Nakama device auth, the gateway hop, a direct game-server join, and replicated entities reconciled into Burst-compiled ISystem simulation with Entities.Graphics rendering. Includes auto-attack combat, a gold/leaderboard economy, a map selector, and an on-screen HUD for connection state, RTT and server health. Needs a running backend.

Drives a synthetic 15 Hz snapshot stream into the remote-interpolation core — no server, no network — and renders it beside the reset-on-arrival algorithm 0.19.0 replaced, so an early arrival, a late arrival and a dropped snapshot can be seen rather than read about. Buttons inject each perturbation, a slider pushes arrival jitter past the 100 ms buffer, and the readout reports frame step, largest step, backward steps and render delay.
Fetches game content from a running game server over /content, caches it by hash, and lists every item with the source it came from. Second run reads CACHE, which is the 304 path working.

Two synthetic clocks, no server, no network: a dial sets how fast the client's clock runs against the server's, SnapshotStalenessEstimator fits the ratio from snapshot arrivals alone, and the prediction clock steers on it. Convergence, refusal past the clamp, a stalled frame and a stepped server clock can each be seen rather than read about. 'Raise delivery floor' is the one to press: it adds a sustained delivery delay while leaving the two clocks in perfect agreement, and the fit reports tens of thousands of ppm anyway — the defect v0.34.0 closes. Watch corroborated stay NO and both the clock rate and the age refuse to follow it. The +110,000 ppm dial default was once recorded as this machine's measured ratio; it has been falsified (220 ppm idle) and is kept as a synthetic stress case at the clamp boundary.

NetworkClient built through RegisterNetworking() in a VContainer scope, against a live backend: authenticate, join, then break the connection on purpose — kill the game-session transport, starve the heartbeat until PongTimeout, or close as the user — and watch the reconnect policy decide (PeerClosed/HeartbeatTimeout reconnect inside the 60 s budget with attempt n/N and backoff; a user close never does). Live panel for state, generation, elapsed budget and every ReconnectProgress event. Needs a running backend and VContainer.

Synthetic world, no server, no network: one observer with an AOI radius over hundreds to thousands of entities, with the visible set computed twice per frame - once by the plain scan, once by narrowing with a uniform grid - and the two answers compared live. Shows entities-in-view versus total, the observer's radius, how many entities each strategy examined, and whether the server's occupancy gate would use its index at this density. The mismatch counter is the point: narrowing the search must not change who is visible.

A synthetic crowd through the game server's per-connection downlink budget, no server and no network: dial the population and how much of it moves, watch snapshot bytes flatten against the cap, entities get deferred oldest-first, and the client go a beat stale — while the 'handle errors' readout stays at zero, which is the invariant that makes shedding safe. Byte figures are measured from real Protobuf snapshots.

Two KCP state machines back-to-back, no server, no network. Sends messages through the ARQ with configurable packet loss and renders the results on screen: reliable delivery, fragmentation/reassembly, and retransmission under loss — all visible rather than read about.

No server, no network. A synthetic snapshot stream drives the real codec, resolver, merger and view binder while an attacker swings at a victim. Two buttons are the whole scene. 'Stop sending events': HP keeps falling because HP is state, and the floating damage numbers stop because a number is an occurrence -- press 'Heal the victim' at the same time and a hit and a heal net out inside one tick, so there is no HP delta a damage number could have been derived from. 'Stop sending action_seq': the attacker keeps attacking and the SWING flash fires once and then stops, while action reads Attacking on every snapshot -- the repeated-attack problem reproduced on demand, and the reason the retrigger edge has to be manufactured by the server. A third button sends an event naming an entity this client was never told about: the resolver counts the unresolved participant, still renders the number with no source, and does NOT abort the snapshot, which is the deliberate asymmetry with an unresolvable entity handle.

No server, no network. A synthetic snapshot stream drives the real codec, resolver, merger and view binder: three capsules orbit a ring and point along their direction of travel, and that direction arrives only in facing_brad — nothing in the scene derives it from movement. Press 'Stop sending facing' and they keep moving and stop turning, holding the last heading instead of snapping to east, which is the 'zero means not sent' rule made visible and the reason facing is a biased integer rather than a float. Three buttons also run a real JoinTokenResponse through the client's version rule: a matching server is admitted, a skewed one is refused with the named reason protocol_version_mismatch and marked permanent, and one that advertises nothing is admitted on trust and says so.

Two peers in one process running ADR-22's transport crypto and ADR-25's server identity for real -- no server, no network, no sockets. Fresh X25519 ephemerals authenticated by a join-token-derived binding, HKDF-SHA256 to two one-direction keys, ChaCha20-Poly1305 per frame with the sequence as the nonce, and an Ed25519 identity key the 'server' generates per session and signs the transcript with. Every frame is shown twice: the plaintext the game wrote, and the bytes a capture would get. Eight buttons each mount an attack -- a flipped bit, a byte-perfect replay, a replayed header with a garbage body (the counter must not move), a cleartext Envelope, a peer with the wrong JOIN_TOKEN_SECRET, a man in the middle who swaps an ephemeral key, a flipped signature byte, and a substituted identity key re-signed with the attacker's own private half. That last one is the only button whose honest answer depends on a setting, and the 'gateway hop authenticated' toggle is the lesson of the scene: it changes the verdict WITHOUT changing the signature, because the identity key arrives on the gateway hop and a signature over a key an attacker supplied proves nothing. It does NOT prove a real server behaves this way -- both peers are this process -- and the ADR-22 binding it exercises can never be verified by a shipped client, because that would require the key that mints join tokens.

Dungeon entry (ADR-26) asked for by the real NetworkClient against a gateway the scene starts itself, reporting the bytes actually sent. The backend half was proven by a Go probe -- which proves a server and says nothing about whether the shipped client can reach it, and for a while it could not, because the client's wire had no party_id at all. Four cases: a map entry OMITS party_id rather than sending "" (the backend uses omitempty and the golden vectors compare bytes across both implementations); a dungeon entry carries it; an empty party id throws before a socket is opened rather than falling back to a map; and every reconnect attempt carries the SAME party id -- a rejoin that forgets it asks for a map named after the dungeon content, so the player silently leaves their party behind. It does NOT prove a party exists, that Nakama's RPCs work, or that your gateway allocates anything.

The client half of ADR-23, run for real against listeners the scene starts itself. One case connects over TLS with a pinned certificate and round-trips a frame; the other four are REFUSALS, because a TLS switch that quietly yields a plaintext link -- or a validation callback that returns true -- reads exactly like a working one everywhere else: an unpinned connection to a self-signed certificate must be refused by the platform trust store, a TLS client against a plaintext gateway must not downgrade, a plaintext client against a TLS gateway must not get a usable frame, and the transport factory asked for TcpTls with no TlsOptions must throw rather than hand back cleartext. It does NOT prove your gateway is configured for TLS, and says nothing about Android.

No server, no network. One synthetic attacker written at the server's CRITICAL rate and sampled at its WORLD rate, encoded as real Protobuf snapshots and merged by the real resolver -- twice, once with the server's one-shot latch and once without it. The second column is the server as it behaved before the latch shipped: roughly three quarters of attacks never reach a client at all, because only one base tick in four is ever sampled and the next tick of movement overwrites Attacking before anyone can see it. Both arms receive the same snapshots and the same bytes -- action_seq is a varint on a message that was being sent anyway -- and what differs is how many attacks were in one. The counter rule is the real shared one (ActionStateLogic.Advance) and the bytes are built the way the server builds them; the LATCH is mirrored rather than imported, because a client has no tick schedule to apply it to, and that is the scene's honest limit.

No server, no network. A synthetic population encoded twice into real Protobuf snapshots -- once as the game server sends today, once with distance- and type-tiered send intervals -- so the saving can be seen against the shape of world that produces it. That is the point: the saving is a property of the POPULATION, not of the feature. Press Cluster, the shape the published 200-player ceiling was measured on, and the answer is 0.0% -- every entity is a near player, every entity is tier 1, and no weighting demotes any of them. Press Realistic and it is 44-46%, at a worst case of 200ms staleness. Both are true, and which one gets quoted decides whether the feature is worth building. Bytes are real (CalculateSize on the generated wire types, including handle interning and keyframe resets); the encoder's selection logic is MIRRORED, and GameServer.Tests/Bench/ImportanceIntervalBench.cs runs the real one and is the number of record -- this scene reproduces its four reference rows to within 2% on bytes and 0.4 points on savings. Two sliders are there to attack the headline figure: drag mob-moving to 1 (an idle entity is already free, so much of the saving is the tiering taking credit for delta suppression) and drag the AOI radius (the competing lever, already shipped, and a square law).
